To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the metal-insulator transition in a two-dimensional electron gas with nearly periodic potential is continuous and that the conductivity in the metallic phase is finite and equal to $\sigma\sim2e^2/\hbar$.
(1) the metal-insulator transition in two dimensions can be controlled by a periodic potential, and (2) the transition is continuous in presence of disorder.
the two-dimensional metal-insulator transition in a nearly periodic (i.e., weakly modulated) potential is controlled by the modulation of the periodic component of the potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electronic structure and transport properties of a 2D system of noninteracting electrons with a nearly periodic potential.
the metal-insulator transition in two dimensions in the presence of disorder, and with the effect of a periodic potential on this transition.
the interplay between the charge density wave and the disorder in the two-dimensional electron gas at zero temperature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the metal-insulator transition in a nearly periodic two-dimensional potential is a continuous transition with a non-vanishing density of states at the Fermi surface and a finite conductivity.
a two-dimensional electron gas in a periodic plus weak random potential is always metallic.
the metal-insulator transition in a 2D electron gas in a nearly periodic (i.e. a weak random) potential is a continuous transition, which is controlled by the modulation of the periodic component.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have studied a metal-insulator-transition in two dimensions, which is continuous in the absence of randomness.
the metal-insulator transition in two dimensions is not a phase transition, but a crossover from a weak to a strong localization regime, and that the dc conductivity is a smooth function of disorder.
the metal-insulator transition is controlled by the modulation of the periodic part of the potential, and not by the amplitude of the random part.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a metal-insulator (Mott) transition can be induced by a nearly periodic potential.
the metal-insulator transition in two dimensions can be driven by a periodic potential alone, in the absence of any interaction.
the metal-insulator transition in a nearly periodic system is a continuous transition.
